title: The effects of plyometric versus resistance training on running economy and 5-km running time in middle-aged recreational runners
authors: Eihara Y, Takao K, Sugiyama T, Maeo S, Kanehisa H, Isaka T
population: Middle-aged recreational runners randomized to plyometric (n=10) or resistance training (n=10); oxygen cost assessed at 8-12 km/h
findings: Both programs ran twice per week for 10 weeks alongside daily running; resistance training used leg press, leg curl and calf raise at 50-90% of 1RM.
Both groups improved countermovement jump height (6.4-8.3%) and oxygen cost regardless of running velocity (2.0%, p = 0.001), without group differences.
Resistance training increased 1RM on all three lifts (19.0-21.1%); plyometrics increased leg curl 1RM only (8.5%).
Neither group changed 5-km time (p 0.259 or higher).
The change in calf raise 1RM correlated with the change in oxygen cost (r = -0.477, p = 0.046).
limitations: Only 20 participants and no running-only control group, so the economy gain cannot be separated from running or familiarization effects; mean age not stated in the abstract; 10 weeks only; no performance effect.
implications: For recreational and middle-aged runners either plyometric or resistance training twice weekly is acceptable; let preference and injury history decide.
Include calf and plantarflexor strengthening explicitly.
Do not promise a 5 km time improvement from a 10-week block in recreational runners; about 2% oxygen-cost improvement is the supported expectation.

verification.notes: Crossref and Europe PMC re-fetched. Added resistance-training lifts and loads from abstract.
